passages.title: What Happens Inside a Loaf
passages.passage: Bread looks like the simplest of foods, yet what goes on inside a loaf is anything but simple. When flour is mixed with water, two proteins that had been lying dormant in the grain begin to link together, forming a stretchy network known (1)____ gluten. Knead the dough and the network tightens; leave it alone and it relaxes. Bakers speak of 'developing' the dough, and it is this network, (2)____ than the yeast, that decides whether the finished loaf will hold its shape. The yeast, for its part, feeds on the sugars in the flour and gives (3)____ carbon dioxide, which the gluten traps in thousands of tiny pockets. Had the network been weak, the gas would simply have escaped, and the loaf would have come out of the oven as flat as a biscuit. It is only when the dough goes into the oven (4)____ the real drama begins. In the first few minutes the trapped gas expands rapidly, a process bakers refer to (5)____ oven spring, and the loaf can grow by a third before the crust sets. Meanwhile the starch absorbs water and stiffens, and the sugars on the surface turn brown, releasing the smell that draws people into a bakery (6)____ the street. Not until the last century (7)____ scientists understand these reactions in detail; before that, the craft was passed on by hand. Even now, a good baker relies (8)____ much on touch as on thermometers. (9)____ the bread has cooled, one final change takes place: the starch slowly recrystallises, which is (10)____ a loaf goes stale even when it is kept perfectly dry.

questions.explanation: The passive collocation is known as + a name. Known for would introduce a quality something is famous for, and known by needs a person who knows.

X rather than Y sets one candidate against another inside the cleft sentence; more than the yeast (to a greater degree than the yeast) is an equally natural comparison of degree. Other than means apart from, and less than would credit the yeast instead.
To give off a gas or smell is to release it; give out is also used of heat and gas. Give up means to abandon and give away means to donate, neither of which fits.
The cleft structure It is only when … that … needs that to introduce the main clause. Which or when would leave the sentence without a main clause at all.
You refer to something as a name. Refer to it by is possible only with by the name of, and refer to it for means consult it for information.

People are drawn into the bakery from the street, the place they start; off the street is the informal equivalent, and across/down the street also fit by placing the bakery relative to the passer-by. To the street would reverse the direction, and in the street is an awkward description of where a shop is.

After fronted Not until … the subject and auxiliary invert, so did scientists understand is required. Have would clash with the last century, a finished period, and without inversion the sentence is ungrammatical.
The comparison of equality is as much on X as on Y, so the first as is needed. So much is only used in this pattern after a negative, and too much would mean excessively.

Once (or after, when) the bread has cooled introduces the moment the final change starts. Until would make the change stop at that point, and while would place it during the cooling rather than after it.
Which is why presents the recrystallising as the reason for the loaf going stale. Which is how would describe a method, and which is because reverses cause and effect.

passages.title: Farming on the Slopes of Fire
passages.passage: Few landscapes look less promising for farming than the slopes of a volcano, yet some of the most densely settled countryside on earth lies precisely there. The explanation, (1)____ it turns out, is in the ash. When a volcano erupts, it throws out rock that has been ground into fine particles, each of them rich (2)____ potassium, phosphorus and a dozen other minerals that plants crave. Ordinary soil takes centuries to build (3)____ such reserves; a single eruption can deliver them in an afternoon. No sooner (4)____ the ash cooled than rain begins to break it down, releasing the minerals in a form that roots can absorb. The result is land so fertile that farmers on the flanks of certain volcanoes harvest three crops a year, (5)____ their neighbours a valley away manage only one. It is hardly surprising, (6)____, that people keep returning to places that have been destroyed more than once within living memory. The risk is real, but so (7)____ the reward, and for a family with little land the choice is not a difficult one. Governments have tried to move such communities to safer ground, usually (8)____ little success; the villagers drift back within a generation. Geologists like to point (9)____ that the very ash which buried a town in one century may be feeding its orchards in the next. Had the mountain never erupted, the valley (10)____ today be as poor as any other in the region.

questions.explanation: The parenthetical comment is as it turns out, meaning as we discover. So it turns out would have to stand as its own clause, and if it turns out makes the explanation uncertain, which the passage does not intend.
Something is rich in the minerals it contains. Rich with is occasionally seen in literary style but not with a list of chemical elements, and rich of does not exist.
To build up reserves is to accumulate them gradually. Build on means to use something as a foundation, and build in means to include as a fixed part.

The inverted No sooner has X happened than Y happens describes a general, repeated sequence, so the present perfect has is needed after the fronted adverb; no sooner is the ash cooled, treating cooled as a state, is also possible. Had would shift the whole account into a single past occasion, which the present tense begins rules out.

While or whereas sets the three harvests against the neighbours' single one; concessive though/although makes the same contrast. But cannot follow a comma inside this sentence without a subject change, and because would make the neighbours' poor harvest the cause of the good one.

Then (or therefore) between commas draws the conclusion from the fertility just described; a hedging perhaps also fits the slot. However would signal a contrast, and too would add a second surprising thing when none has been mentioned.
So + auxiliary + subject repeats the previous verb for a new subject: the risk is real, but so is the reward. Does would need a full verb to stand in for, and are disagrees with the singular reward.

An attempt is made with little success; the preposition describes the result that accompanies the action. In success and at success are not English, and for little success would mean the success was the aim.
To point out that something is true is to draw attention to it. Point to takes a noun, not a that-clause, and point at is a physical gesture.

This is a mixed conditional: a past condition (had the mountain never erupted) with a present result marked by today, so would (or the more tentative might/could) + bare infinitive is needed. Would have been would place the result in the past, which today contradicts, and will cannot follow an unreal condition.

passages.title: The Business of Birdsong
passages.passage: Anyone who has been woken by a blackbird at four in the morning might reasonably ask what the bird thinks it is doing. For a long time the answer seemed obvious: birds sing because they are happy. Only in the last century (1)____ scientists begin to test that assumption, and what they found was far more interesting. Song, it turns out, is mostly a matter of business. A male sings, first of all, to lay (2)____ to a territory; every phrase is a warning to rivals that the trees around him are already taken. He sings, secondly, to attract a mate, and here the quality of the performance matters a great deal. Females of many species prefer males (3)____ repertoires are larger, on the grounds that a bird which has learned many songs has probably lived long enough to do so. The dawn chorus, (4)____, is less a celebration than a daily announcement that the singer has made it through the night. (5)____ does the story end there. Young birds learn their songs much as children learn speech, by listening to adults and then practising, badly (6)____ first, until the phrases come out cleanly. A chick raised in silence will grow up with a thin, incomplete song, (7)____ matter how healthy it is. Some species even develop local dialects, so that a bird from one valley can be told (8)____ from one a few miles away. Whether birds take any pleasure in all this is a question science cannot answer. (9)____ we can say is that the singing is neither idle nor accidental, and that the blackbird outside the window is doing far more (10)____ simply greeting the sun.

questions.explanation: A fronted restrictive phrase such as Only in the last century forces inversion, so the auxiliary did must come before scientists. Have is tempting because of the last century, but the following verb begin is a bare infinitive and the account continues in the past.
To lay claim to something is to assert that it is yours, which is exactly what a territorial song does. Lay hold of means to seize physically, and lay title to is not a fixed expression.

The relative pronoun shows possession: the repertoires belong to the males, so whose is needed. Which and that would require repertoires to be the subject of the clause without an owner, and of which is two words in the wrong order here.

Then (or therefore) between commas signals that this sentence sums up the two reasons just given. However would contradict them, and too would add the chorus as a further example rather than a conclusion.

Nor does the story end there is an inverted negative adding a further point after previous negatives. Not cannot begin a clause with an auxiliary inverted like this, and never would mean the story is endless.
The fixed phrase is at first, meaning in the early stages. In first and on first do not exist as adverbials, and from first would need the.
No matter how + adjective means regardless of how healthy it is. Not matter is ungrammatical, and whatever cannot be followed by matter how.
To tell one thing apart from another is to distinguish them. Tell off means to scold, and tell away is not an English phrasal verb.

What we can say is … is a pseudo-cleft that puts the whole statement in focus; All we can say works the same way with a hint of limitation. That we can say is not a noun clause, and Which needs an antecedent.
The comparative far more than requires than. Far more as is not a comparison, and far more of would need a noun rather than an -ing form after it.

passages.title: A Room for Strangers
passages.passage: Long before coffee reached Europe, the tea house had already become a fixture of city life across much of Asia. The earliest ones, (1)____ far as records show, were little more than roadside stalls where travellers could rest and refill a flask. Within a few centuries, however, they had grown (2)____ something much grander: rooms with painted screens, musicians in the corner and a proprietor who knew every customer by name. Merchants struck deals there, poets exchanged verses, and matchmakers arranged marriages over a pot that (3)____ be refilled a dozen times before anyone stood up to leave. What made the tea house unusual was that it belonged to nobody in particular. A scholar and a porter might sit at neighbouring tables, (4)____ they would never have shared a room anywhere else. Rulers were not always comfortable with this. More than one emperor tried to close the tea houses (5)____ the grounds that too much talk was going on inside them, and more than one failed, (6)____ a city deprived of its tea houses quickly became restless. Only when the trade routes shifted (7)____ the great tea houses begin to decline; rival drinks arrived, and the young preferred novelty. Yet the institution never quite disappeared. In many cities today the old houses are being restored, (8)____ least in part by people who have never drunk tea from a lidded cup in their lives. Had the tea house merely sold tea, it would have vanished long (9)____. It survived because it sold something rarer: a place (10)____ strangers could sit as equals.

questions.explanation: As far as records show limits the claim to what the evidence supports; so far as is an accepted variant. Too far as and how far as are not fixed expressions.
To grow into something is to develop until you become it. Grow to is used with an infinitive (grow to love) or a size, and grow up is used of children, not institutions.

The pot might (or could, would) be refilled: a past habit or possibility described from the narrator's viewpoint. May and can are present forms that clash with the past narrative, and must would turn a custom into an obligation.

The clause contrasts what happened inside the tea house with what would never happen outside it, so a concessive or contrastive linker (though, although, whereas, while, or contrastive when) is needed. Because would make the sharing a result of the refusal, and so gets the logic backwards.
The justification for an action is given on the grounds that. For the grounds and with the grounds are not English, and in the grounds would refer to the land around a building.

The clause explains why the emperors failed, so a reason linker is required: literary for, or because, since, as. So would make the restlessness a consequence of the failure rather than its cause, and while would introduce a contrast that is not there.

After a fronted Only when … clause, the main clause inverts: did the great tea houses begin. Had would need a past participle rather than begin, and the uninverted the tea houses began cannot follow the fronted phrase.
At least in part means partly, if not more. In least and for least do not exist, and not least would mean especially, which does not fit before in part.
Long ago (or long since, long before) places the imagined disappearance well in the past, completing the third conditional. Long after would need a reference event, and long already is not English.

The relative adverb where links a place to the clause that describes what happens in it. Which would need a preposition (in which), and that cannot replace in which after place when no preposition follows.

passages.title: Men Who Cut Through Hills
passages.passage: When the first railway tunnels were driven through the hills of northern England, nobody involved had done anything like it before. The engineers had drawings; the men who actually cut the rock had (1)____ but their hands, a few tools and an enormous amount of nerve. Work went on around the clock, gangs (2)____ over from one another every twelve hours, and progress was measured in feet. Had the two teams digging from opposite ends missed each other (3)____ even a few yards, the whole scheme would have been a laughing stock. In the event they met almost exactly (4)____ planned, a feat of surveying that still impresses engineers today. The dangers were constant. Water broke in without warning, roofs collapsed, and the candles the men worked (5)____ frequently went out, leaving them in darkness a mile underground. Casualties were high, and it is only recently that historians have begun to put names to those (6)____ lives the tunnels cost. What the men were paid was, by the standards of the day, generous; what they endured (7)____ earn it was not. Contractors pushed relentlessly, since their own fortunes depended (8)____ speed, and inspectors rarely visited. Yet by all accounts morale among the gangs remained remarkably high, partly out of pride in the work and partly because there was nowhere (9)____ to go. The tunnels are still in use. Trains pass through them at speeds their builders could scarcely have imagined, and hardly (10)____ of the passengers gives a thought to how the passage was made.

questions.explanation: Nothing but means only; little but softens it slightly and is also acceptable. Anything but means the opposite of, and everything but would mean the men had all except their hands.
To take over from someone is to replace them on duty; the participle taking fits the absolute clause. Handing over describes the gang leaving, not the one arriving, and getting over means recovering.
The margin of an error or difference is expressed with by: missed by a few yards. For a few yards would give a distance travelled, and with a few yards makes no sense of the measurement.
As planned is the reduced form of as it had been planned; where planned stresses the location and is also defensible. Like planned is non-standard, and than planned needs a comparative before it.

You work by candlelight, the source of illumination, so the stranded preposition in the reduced relative clause is by. With would suggest the candles were tools, and under would need the candles to be above the men.

The lives belonged to the men, so the possessive relative whose is needed: those whose lives the tunnels cost. Which and that cannot show possession, and who would leave lives without a link to those.
The infinitive of purpose to earn it explains why they endured what they did. For earn is ungrammatical before a verb, and and earn would make the earning a separate hardship.
The verb is depend on (or the more formal upon). Depend of is a common error borrowed from other languages, and depend from is not English.
Nowhere else means no other place. Nowhere other requires than and a comparison, and nowhere more would need an adjective.
Hardly any of the passengers means almost none, and the singular verb gives treats the group as a quantity. Hardly some and hardly no are ungrammatical, and hardly one of is not idiomatic.

passages.title: A Cloud at Ground Level
passages.passage: Fog is simply a cloud that has lost its way, or rather one that has formed at ground level instead of high above it. Air always holds some water vapour, and the warmer the air, the (1)____ vapour it can carry. When that air cools, it eventually reaches the point (2)____ which it can hold no more, and the surplus condenses into droplets so small that they hang in the air rather than falling. Whether this happens on a clear night, after a shower or over the sea depends (3)____ how the cooling takes place. The most familiar kind forms on calm, cloudless nights, when the ground loses heat to the sky and chills the layer of air (4)____ contact with it. By dawn a valley may be filled to the brim, (5)____ the hilltops around it are already in sunshine. Coastal fog behaves differently: warm, moist air drifts over a cold current and cools from below, sometimes for days (6)____ end. Cities once suffered a third kind, in which smoke provided the particles (7)____ which droplets could gather. So thick did this become at times (8)____ buses had to be led through the streets by men on foot. Fog rarely lasts long once the sun is up, (9)____ the same air that produced it warms again and reabsorbs the droplets. Forecasters can now predict it with fair accuracy, (10)____ a night of fog still brings airports to a standstill more often than most travellers would like.

questions.q: Blank (1): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: The double comparative the warmer …, the more … links two changes that rise together. Most is a superlative, and much and many are not comparative forms.

questions.q: Blank (2): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Something happens at a point, so the relative phrase is the point at which. In which would suit a period or a state, and on and by do not collocate with point in this sense.

questions.q: Blank (3): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: The verb is depend on, and the preposition is kept before an indirect question (depends on how). Depend of is a frequent learner error, and in and from never follow depend.

questions.q: Blank (4): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Two things touching are in contact with each other. On contact means at the moment of touching, which changes the sense, and at and by do not form the phrase.

questions.q: Blank (5): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: While introduces a clause that contrasts the foggy valley with the sunny hilltops. During and despite are prepositions and cannot take a clause, and meanwhile is an adverb that cannot join two clauses after a comma.

questions.q: Blank (6): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: For days on end means for many days without a break. At an end means finished, in the end means finally, and to end is not an idiom of duration.

questions.q: Blank (7): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Droplets gather around a particle, which acts as a core. About in this sense is archaic, over suggests covering a surface, and under puts the droplets beneath the particle.

questions.q: Blank (8): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: The inverted structure So thick did it become that … introduces the result with that. Than belongs with comparatives, as would need as thick as, and a second so has no role here.

questions.q: Blank (9): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: The clause explains why fog clears, so a reason linker, since, is needed. So would make the warming a result of the clearing, unless makes it a condition that prevents it, and whereas signals a contrast that is not intended.

questions.q: Blank (10): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Good forecasts and airports still stopping are in contrast, which yet expresses after a comma. So and for would present the standstill as a consequence or a reason, and nor needs a preceding negative and inversion.
